title: Life Insurance Profitability & Cashflow Modelling
summary: Developed an Excel-based actuarial model to evaluate the expected profitability of a 20-year unit-linked life insurance policy, incorporating multiple decrement modelling, cashflow projections and surrender timing sensitivity analysis.
description: This project investigates the expected profitability of a 20-year unit-linked term assurance policy issued to an individual aged 58. The policy is subject to three competing causes of termination: death, redundancy and voluntary surrender. An actuarial model was developed in Excel to update the multiple decrement assumptions, project unit fund values and insurer cashflows, and evaluate the expected present value of profit. The analysis also examines how accelerating surrender benefit payments affects profitability, using the claims acceleration approximation under a uniform surrender assumption.
objective: To calculate the expected present value of profit and profit margin for a unit-linked life insurance policy under revised decrement assumptions, and assess the impact of alternative surrender benefit payment schedules on expected profitability.
methodology: Updated an existing multiple decrement table by reducing the underlying force of mortality by 8% and increasing the force of surrender by 5%, while keeping redundancy rates unchanged. Assumed independent decrements with constant forces within each year of age.
Projected the unit fund over the 20-year policy term, incorporating annual premiums, a 65% allocation rate, a 3% bid-offer spread, a 1.1% annual management charge and time-varying investment returns.
Constructed an Excel cashflow model incorporating premium income, expenses, interest, policy charges and expected death, redundancy and surrender benefit payments.
Calculated the expected present value of profit using a 5% annual risk discount rate and determined the profit margin relative to the expected present value of premiums.
Applied the claims acceleration approximation to model surrender benefits payable at the end of progressively shorter intervals, assuming surrender occurs uniformly throughout each policy year.
Evaluated payment frequencies of 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64 intervals per year, alongside annual and immediate surrender payment scenarios, while holding other cashflow assumptions unchanged.
Compared the resulting profit estimates and visualised the relationship between surrender payment frequency and expected profitability.
findings: Calculated a baseline expected present value of profit of £5,083.60.
Determined an expected present value of premiums of £15,151.66, producing a baseline profit margin of 33.55%.
Found that accelerating surrender benefit payments progressively reduced the expected present value of profit.
Under the claims acceleration approximation, immediate surrender payments produced an expected present value of profit of £5,057.36, a reduction of £26.24 compared with annual payments.
Demonstrated that the policy maintained a positive expected present value of profit across all surrender payment schedules considered, under the specified modelling assumptions.
Identified surrender payment timing as a factor affecting expected profitability, with earlier payments increasing the accumulated value of expected benefit outgo and associated expenses.

title: Multivariate Statistical Analysis of International Athletics Performance
summary: Conducted a multivariate statistical analysis of national athletics records across 55 countries using R, applying Hotelling's T² hypothesis tests, linear transformations and simultaneous confidence intervals to investigate relationships between race distance, performance and country classification.
description: This project investigates national record times for men's 100m, 200m, 400m and 800m track events across 55 countries immediately prior to the 1984 Olympic Games. The analysis addresses two primary questions: whether average race times scale proportionally with distance, and whether athletics performance differs between countries according to their historical economic classification. Statistical analysis was conducted in R, incorporating exploratory data visualisation, multivariate normality assumptions, one-sample and two-sample Hotelling's T² tests, and simultaneous confidence intervals. The findings identify significant differences in average speed across race distances and an association between country classification and national athletics records.
objective: To investigate whether mean athletics record times increase proportionally with race distance and assess whether the multivariate mean performance differs between developed and less-developed countries, using Hotelling's T² hypothesis tests and simultaneous confidence intervals.
methodology: Imported national athletics records for 55 countries and converted 800m race times from minutes to seconds to ensure consistent measurement units across all four events.
Generated descriptive statistics, including means, medians and interquartile ranges, and scaled race times to a common 800m distance to compare performance and variability across events.
Constructed pairwise scatterplots with 95% normal data ellipses to explore relationships between race times and assess the reasonableness of bivariate normality assumptions.
Formulated a hypothesis that mean race times scale proportionally with distance and constructed a linear transformation matrix to express the hypothesis as a zero-mean vector.
Implemented a one-sample Hotelling's T^2 test in R, converting the test statistic to an F-statistic to evaluate the joint proportionality hypothesis.
Calculated simultaneous confidence intervals for the transformed mean differences to identify which relationships between race distances contributed to rejection of the null hypothesis.
Compared athletics records between developed and less-developed countries using boxplots and a two-sample Hotelling's T^2 test with a pooled covariance matrix.
Constructed simultaneous confidence intervals for the differences between country-group mean vectors to determine which individual race distances exhibited statistically significant differences.
findings: Found that mean race times did not increase proportionally with distance, rejecting the joint proportionality hypothesis with a one-sample Hotelling's T^2 test.
Identified statistically significant departures from proportionality between the 200m and 400m events and between the 400m and 800m events using simultaneous confidence intervals.
Found that the proportional relationship between mean 100m and 200m times was not statistically rejected at the 5% significance level.
Observed lower median national record times and generally narrower interquartile ranges among developed countries across the four track events.
Identified a statistically significant overall difference in mean athletics performance between the two country classifications using a two-sample Hotelling's T^2 test.
Found that the 200m event was the only individual race with a simultaneous confidence interval for the between-group mean difference that excluded zero at the 5% significance level.

Demonstrated the application of multivariate hypothesis testing and simultaneous inference to investigate relationships between correlated performance measures, while recognising the limitations of normality assumptions and observational data.
